title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 43–44 (editorially reviewed)
description: Unit 43 teaches the irregular forms of take, duration patterns, carrying objects, everyday collocations and transport. Unit 44 contrasts bring and take by direction and covers giving, receiving and returning objects. British-English IPA, original English notes and examples, and Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt are provided.
sourceNotice: Teaching pages, illustrations, tips and exercises of both assigned units in the user-provided textbook were inspected. Explanations and example sentences are independently written; exercises and illustrations are not reproduced. Exercise-context entries retain explicit origin labels.

units.title: Unit 43 — Take / took / taken
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 43, printed pages 92–93 (PDF pages 93–94); original examples and explanatory notes.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: The journey took longer than we expected.
items.note: Take is irregular: take (base form), took (past simple), taken (past participle). Its meaning depends on the expression: take the bus, take a photo or take twenty minutes.

items.pt: alguém leva certo tempo para fazer algo
items.example: It takes my sister twenty minutes to walk to work.
items.note: Use It takes + person + amount of time + to + base verb to describe the time needed for an activity. It is an impersonal subject; takes agrees with it.
items.speechText: it takes me ten minutes to walk

items.pt: alguém levou certo tempo para fazer algo
items.example: It took us an hour to finish the project.
items.note: Use It took + person + amount of time + to + base verb for a completed activity in the past. Took is the past simple form of take.
items.speechText: it took me two hours to finish

items.word: How long does it take to ...?
items.example: How long does it take to reach the airport?
items.note: Ask about a usual or expected duration with How long does it take to + verb? After does, use the base form take, not takes.
items.speechText: How long does it take to get there?

items.example: How long did it take you to learn to drive?
items.note: Ask about a past duration with How long did it take? or How long did it take to + verb? Did carries the past tense, so take remains in its base form.
items.speechText: How long did it take to get there?

items.word: it takes + person + time + to get to work
items.pt: levar tempo para chegar ao trabalho
items.example: It takes me thirty minutes to get to work by train.
items.note: This phrase describes the duration of a journey to work: It takes me half an hour to get to work. Do not confuse the whole It takes ... pattern with take time to do something, which can mean make time for it.
items.speechText: it takes me half an hour to get to work

items.word: it took + person + time + to do homework
items.pt: levar tempo para fazer a lição de casa
items.example: It took me two hours to do my homework yesterday.
items.note: For a completed past activity, say It took me two hours to do my homework. Use do homework, not make homework; homework is generally uncountable.
items.speechText: it took me two hours to do my homework

items.word: How long did it take you to ...?
items.ipa: /haʊ lɒŋ dɪd ɪt teɪk ju tə/
items.example: How long did it take you to read that book?
items.note: When asking about a person, place the object pronoun after take: How long did it take you to learn? Use take, not took, after did.
items.speechText: How long did it take you to learn?

items.example: Take your phone with you when you go out.
items.note: Take something with you means carry it when leaving for another place. With you makes it clear that the object accompanies the person.

items.example: Take an umbrella because the sky looks dark.
items.note: An umbrella is something you may need when you go out in the rain. Use take when carrying an item away from the present location.

items.example: We should take some water on our walk.
items.note: Use take some water for carrying water to another place, as on a walk or to the beach. Water is uncountable in this context.

items.example: Take your camera with you on the trip.
items.note: Take your camera means carry the camera to another place; take a photo means use the camera to photograph something. The meanings are different.

items.pt: levar algo para dentro de um lugar
items.example: You cannot take food into the library.
items.note: Use take + object + into + place for movement from outside to inside. The source gives a prohibition on taking a camera into a museum.
items.speechText: take your bag into the room

items.example: Take your passport when you travel abroad.
items.note: A passport is a useful item to take when travelling to another country. This is a suggested answer to the illustrated exercise, not a distinct collocation taught on the presentation page.

items.example: Take your phone so you can send a message later.
items.note: You may take your phone when you need to text someone. This is an example suggested by the phone picture and question in exercise 43.4.

items.example: May I take a photo of this building?
items.note: Say take a photo of a person, place or object. Photo is short for photograph; make a photo is not the normal collocation in this meaning.

items.example: She took a photograph of the mountains.
items.note: Take a photograph means photograph something. It has the same everyday meaning as take a photo, but uses the full noun photograph.

items.example: We took photographs during our visit.
items.note: Use take photographs for making several photographic images. Exercise 43.4 refers to taking photographs and bringing the camera needed for this.

items.example: I am taking an online English course.
items.note: Take a course means enrol on and study a course as a learner. It does not normally mean design or create a course.

items.example: My brother wants to take an English course next year.
items.note: Take an English course is a specific example of take a course. The article an is used before the vowel sound at the beginning of English.

items.pt: fazer uma prova; prestar um exame
items.example: We have to take an exam at the end of the course.
items.note: Take an exam means sit an examination as a candidate. You can also say do an exam in some contexts; make an exam does not usually describe taking a test.

items.example: They take piano lessons on Thursdays.
items.note: Take lessons means receive instruction or attend classes. Compare give lessons, which describes what a teacher does.

items.example: I would like to take Japanese lessons next year.
items.note: Name the subject before lessons: take Japanese lessons or take music lessons. Lessons is plural in this example.

items.example: I take the bus to university every morning.
items.note: Take the bus describes travelling by bus. The is normal with the means of transport in this expression; go by bus is another possibility.

items.example: We took the underground to the museum.
items.note: In British English, the underground is an urban railway system, especially the London Underground. Say take the underground or travel by underground.

items.example: We took a taxi from the station to our hotel.
items.note: Say take a taxi when choosing a taxi as transport. Use the taxi when referring to a particular taxi already known in the context.

items.example: She takes the train to work three times a week.
items.note: Say take the train to describe travelling by train. The phrase appears both in the unit presentation and in its exercises.

items.example: The children take the school bus every morning.
items.note: The picture in exercise 43.3 shows a school bus. This expression is a contextual combination of take + means of transport, rather than a separate phrase explained on the teaching page.

items.example: Can you take a picture of us?
items.note: Take a picture can mean take a photograph. The source lists this phrase as an example of another useful expression with take.

items.example: Please take a look at my notes.
items.note: Take a look at something means look at it, often briefly. The preposition at introduces the thing being examined. This expression is named in the source tip.

items.example: I decided to take a chance and apply for the job.
items.note: Take a chance means try something even though the result is uncertain. The source names the expression in a tip but does not provide a full explanation.

learningObjectives: Recognise the irregular verb forms take, took and taken and use the impersonal pattern It takes or It took + person + time + to + verb.
Ask about the duration of an activity with How long does it take...? and How long did it take you...?.
Use take something with you when carrying things such as an umbrella, water, a camera, a passport or a phone.
Use take something into + place for movement into a place, including restrictions on bringing items inside.
Use take a photo or photograph, take a course, take an exam and take lessons in everyday situations.
Describe travel with take the bus, take the underground, take a taxi and take the train.
Recognise additional expressions listed in the tip: take a picture, take a look at and take a chance.

units.title: Unit 44 — Bring / brought / brought
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 44, printed pages 94–95 (PDF pages 95–96); original examples and explanatory notes.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: She brought her laptop to my house yesterday.
items.note: Bring is irregular: bring (base form), brought (past simple), brought (past participle). Choose bring when the movement is towards the speaker or a relevant destination.

items.pt: trazer (em direção à referência) versus levar (para longe dela)
items.example: Please bring your notes here, but take these letters to the office.
items.note: Bring normally describes movement towards the speaker, the listener or a shared destination; take describes movement away from the reference point. The speaker’s viewpoint matters.

items.example: Could you bring the documents here, please?
items.note: Here means to this place. Use bring something here, without to before here.

items.example: Please take these books there after lunch.
items.note: There means to that place. Use take something there, without to before there; movement is described from the current reference point to another place.

items.pt: levar seus livros para a escola
items.example: Remember to take your books to school tomorrow.
items.note: Say take your books to school when the books leave the present place and go to school with you. To introduces the destination.

items.example: Could you bring me a clean glass from the kitchen?
items.note: Bring + person + object has two objects: bring me a glass. Here the speaker expects the glass to move towards them.

items.example: Could you take this form to the secretary?
items.note: Use take + object + to + recipient when moving something to a person in another place: take a form to the secretary.

items.pt: trazer seu violão; trazer sua guitarra
items.example: Come to my house and bring your guitar.
items.note: In an invitation, bring your guitar means carry it to the place where the speaker will be. Guitar can refer to an acoustic or electric instrument.

items.example: I will bring you a present when I return.
items.note: Bring someone a present means carry a gift to the person. You can also say bring a present to someone.

items.example: She brought fresh vegetables from her garden.
items.note: From introduces the place an item comes from: bring something from the garden. Choose bring if the speaker or other reference point is the destination.
items.speechText: bring some apples from the garden

items.example: Please bring your notebook to class tomorrow.
items.note: Use bring something to + place when that place is the relevant destination, as when a teacher asks students to bring something to a lesson.
items.speechText: bring your notebook to the lesson

items.pt: trazer um pouco de água para alguém
items.example: Can you bring me some water, please?
items.note: The question Can you bring me some water? asks another person to carry water to the speaker. Some works naturally with uncountable water.

items.word: take these papers to the office
items.example: Could you take these papers to the office?
items.note: Take refers to moving the papers from here to the office. The full expression is based on the context in exercise 44.1.

items.example: I brought my friend a small gift.
items.note: Use bring + person + thing without to between the two objects: bring me some apples. Another form is bring something to somebody.

items.example: I brought you some apples from the garden.
items.note: Brought is the past of bring. Use brought you some apples with a plural countable noun; do not form the past as brang.

items.example: She brings her mother flowers every spring.
items.note: Use bring + person + flowers to describe giving flowers carried to someone. With she or he in the present simple, use brings.

items.example: He brought us some chocolates from Belgium.
items.note: Chocolates means individual pieces of chocolate here. The exercises provide contexts for bringing someone some chocolates from a trip.

items.pt: levar comida a uma festa (vista do destino)
items.example: Everyone can bring some food to the party.
items.note: Bring food to a party is natural when considering the party as a shared destination or from the host’s viewpoint. This expression appears in exercise 44.2.

items.example: Take your passport when you travel abroad.
items.note: Take your passport when you travel means carry it with you when leaving. The phrase is reinforced in the matching exercise.

items.example: My sister brought me a book yesterday.
items.note: Brought me + object describes giving or delivering something to the speaker in the past. The fixed spoken part is brought me; complete the pattern with an object.

items.pt: trazer algo de volta; devolver algo ao local de origem
items.example: Please bring my jacket back tomorrow.
items.note: Bring something back means return it to the original place or person, or to a relevant reference point. With a pronoun, say bring it back.

items.example: They brought my umbrella back yesterday.
items.note: Brought something back describes a completed return in the past. With a noun, both brought the book back and brought back the book are possible.

items.word: take something and bring it back
items.pt: levar algo e depois trazê-lo de volta
items.example: You can take my dictionary and bring it back on Monday.
items.note: In a borrowing situation, take something means carry it away and bring it back means return it to the lender. The two verbs reflect opposite movements.

items.example: Take this umbrella, but bring it back tomorrow.
items.note: With a pronoun object, it must come before back: bring it back, not bring back it. Tomorrow identifies when the object should be returned.

items.pt: trazer algo de volta de uma viagem ou lugar
items.example: She brought me some chocolates back from Belgium.
items.note: Bring something back from a place means return with an item obtained there. The expression extends a past-tense example about chocolates from Belgium in exercise 44.4.
items.speechText: bring some chocolates back from Belgium

items.word: take a magazine and bring it back
items.pt: pegar uma revista emprestada e devolvê-la
items.ipa: /teɪk ə ˌmæɡəˈziːn ən brɪŋ ɪt bæk/
items.example: You can take this magazine tonight and bring it back next week.
items.note: In a borrowing situation, you can take a magazine to read and then bring it back to its owner. This scenario is practised in exercise 44.4.

learningObjectives: Recognise the irregular verb forms bring, brought and brought.
Distinguish bring and take according to movement towards or away from the speaker or another reference point.
Use bring + person + object and bring + object + to + person to describe carrying an item to someone.
Use take with movement to another location, such as take your books to school or take a form to the secretary.
Practise bring and take with water, presents, flowers, food, papers, a passport and other items from the textbook exercises.
Use bring something back and bring it back when describing the return of a borrowed item.
Choose bring, brings, brought, take and took where the situation and tense require them.
